guidance.opening:
It is autumn of 1920, in Boston. You are in a landlord’s small office downtown because he sent for someone who might look into a house he cannot keep rented. Papers sit in a neat stack on the desk.

Steven Knott looks you over and does not waste the greeting. “Place I inherited won’t hold a tenant. Last family ran after some kind of disaster, and the neighbors won’t stop talking. I need a pair of eyes on it—find out what’s souring the reputation, daylight work, paid by the day. We’ll talk terms after I know who I’m talking to.”

He taps the stack once, then waits. “So—who are you, and what do you do for a living? Rough answer’s fine.”
guidance.advice: Use listed occupations only. Strong public fits for a 1920s Boston hire to inspect a troubled rental: Journalist, Private Investigator, Police Detective, Police Officer, Lawyer, Librarian, Professor, Antiquarian, Doctor of Medicine, Author, Parapsychologist, Engineer, Clergy. Others can work if the player explains a plausible daylight skill (Artist sketching the place, Dilettante with time, Soldier between jobs). Skip anachronistic Hacker. Useful training: Library Use, Law, History, Persuade, Fast Talk, Spot Hidden, Listen, Psychology, Locksmith or Mechanical Repair for a house, First Aid. Languages: English is assumed; Latin or Italian can be optional flavor, not required. Era belongings: overcoat, notebook, pencil, streetcar fare, modest lodgings—no keys, retainer, or house address yet. Public involvement: hired-by-the-day investigator, reporter, clerk, or concerned professional answering a landlord’s notice; do not treat the job as already accepted. Optional ties (player-chosen, not facts): knew a former tenant, read a rumor, owes a favor, needs the wage. Optional motivation questions in conversation only—why they answered the summons, how they feel about empty houses—not a questionnaire. Preserve uncertainty: neighbors talk, last family fled; no secret identities or solutions.
guidance.handoff: The visitor has met landlord Steven Knott in his Boston office in autumn 1920. Knott has described a hard-to-rent inherited house, a last family driven out, and a possible by-the-day look into what is souring its name, then asked who the visitor is and what they do. Identity and occupation are still being established. No commission has been accepted and no keys, cash, or address have been given. Continue the setup conversation from this meeting until the character card is complete.
